meta.homeTitle: Horus Flow · Botnet detection and traffic visibility for ISPs
meta.homeDescription: Find out which of your ISP's subscribers are in a botnet before your network ends up on a blocklist. MikroTik IPFIX over WireGuard, explainable findings and RouterOS commands.
meta.buyDescription: Request a Horus Flow license: pick a plan and billing period and get your reference number and quote.
meta.ogAlt: Horus Flow NOC wall showing traffic, active subscribers and open findings (simulated data)

hero.title: Find out which subscribers are in a botnet before your network ends up on a blocklist.
hero.lead: Horus Flow reads IPFIX flows from your MikroTik routers, recognizes each subscriber by IP and tells you which one is talking to command-and-control servers, scanning, joining a DDoS or sending spam. With its reasons and the RouterOS commands to act on it.
hero.note: Horus only reads and alerts: it never writes to your router.
hero.gridDesc: Illustration: each dot is a subscriber in 10.20.1.0/24. One of them, 10.20.1.47, is flagged as infected with 94% confidence.
hero.reason: Talks to a command-and-control server listed on Feodo Tracker

problem.title: One infected subscriber costs the whole ISP

blacklist.title: Blocklists
blacklist.body: When an IP on your network sends spam or attacks, reputation lists can block your addresses, and the trouble reaches subscribers who did nothing wrong.

abuse.title: Abuse reports without context
abuse.body: They arrive late, with an IP and a timestamp. Finding the subscriber, and knowing whether they are really compromised, is up to you.

link.title: Traffic nobody asked for
link.body: Outbound scans and attacks eat your uplink and fill your tickets before anyone in the NOC sees them coming.

problem.solutionTitle: Horus Flow tells you who, why and what to do

who.title: Who
who.body: Every IP seen in the flows is a subscriber, discovered automatically. Even behind the router's NAT, thanks to IPFIX post-NAT fields.

why.title: Why
why.body: Nine detectors and reputation lists such as abuse.ch and Spamhaus DROP. Every finding explains its reasons and its confidence.

what.title: What to do
what.body: RouterOS commands to isolate, rate-limit or notify, each with its undo command. You decide and apply them.

features.title: What your NOC sees
features.lead: Real Horus Flow screenshots. The data is simulated: it belongs to no real ISP or subscriber.

mural.title: NOC wall
mural.body: Modular dashboards with configurable widgets and a scalable wall view for the screens in the room.
mural.alt: NOC wall: current traffic, active subscribers, open findings by severity, 24-hour traffic, top subscribers and recent findings

infected.title: Infected subscriber, with reasons
infected.body: The Infected status never comes alone: it shows the confidence and why, from the reputation list to the spam pattern.
infected.alt: Subscriber 10.20.1.47 flagged as Infected with 94% confidence and the list of reasons

finding.title: Findings with commands to act
finding.body: What happened, the evidence and what to do: RouterOS commands ready to copy, each with its undo command. Horus runs nothing on your routers.
finding.alt: Detail of a port 23 scanning finding with evidence and recommended actions

router.title: Router onboarding in minutes
router.body: Horus generates the RouterOS script: a router-initiated WireGuard tunnel, a one-time token and a read-only user. In under 2 minutes the router shows as Exporting.
router.alt: Router connection step with the RouterOS onboarding script generated by Horus

kiosk.title: Kiosk for wall screens
kiosk.body: Each screen is enrolled as a device with a one-time code, read-only and, if you want, with subscriber IPs hidden.
kiosk.alt: One-time code to enroll a kiosk screen, valid for 10 minutes

mobile.title: On your phone too
mobile.body: The same console on small screens, to check a finding wherever you are.
mobile.alt: Scanning finding on a phone, in light mode

more.alerts: Email, Telegram and LibreNMS alerts, configured per ISP. Email and Telegram carry no subscriber IPs by default.
more.ipv6: IPv4 and IPv6 as separate subscribers; IPv6 grouped by delegated prefix (/64 by default).
more.multi: Multi-ISP by design: each provider isolated in data, API, events and permissions.
more.reputation: Reputation lists: abuse.ch Feodo and ThreatFox, Spamhaus DROP, Tor and any your superadmin adds.

how.title: From the router to your NOC, without touching subscribers
how.lead: All you need is the main router of each node. Nothing to install on your subscribers' devices.
how.diagramTitle: How data flows through Horus Flow
how.diagramDesc: The MikroTik router exports IPFIX through a WireGuard tunnel to the Horus Flow server, which discovers subscribers, stores flows and detects botnets; results reach the NOC as dashboards, kiosk screens and alerts.

router.title: MikroTik
router.body: The node's main router exports IPFIX with NAT fields.

tunnel.title: WireGuard
tunnel.body: Flows and the read-only API travel encrypted to Horus.

horus.title: Horus Flow
horus.body: Discovers subscribers, stores flows and aggregates, and runs detection.

noc.title: Your NOC
noc.body: Dashboards, wall screens and alerts by email, Telegram and LibreNMS.

install.title: One-command install
install.body: On a clean Debian 12 or 13, one script installs everything and starts Horus with the system. Updates are signed, with a mandatory backup first and automatic rollback if anything fails.

reliability.title: Reliability measured, not promised
reliability.lead: We tested the whole pipeline by killing components on purpose under constant traffic. These are the results and their conditions.

restart.test: Hard restarts (kill -9 and restart) of the collector, horus-app, NATS and ClickHouse, three times each, at 10,000 flows/s
restart.result: 0 flows lost, 0 duplicates and identical aggregates
restart.note: The only loss is what arrives over UDP while the collector is down; it is measured and shown.

clickhouse.test: ClickHouse down for 5 minutes at 20,000 flows/s
clickhouse.result: 0 loss; the backlog drains in about 2.5 minutes

platform.result: Alerts, findings, sessions, tunnels and kiosk come back on their own in 7–15 s

capacity.result: 10,000 flows/s meeting every criterion on 4 shared vCPUs

reliability.conditions: Test server: a virtual machine with 4 shared vCPUs and 16 GiB, running other workloads at the same time. The figures are a floor, not a ceiling.
reliability.projection: Projection for a 10,000-subscriber ISP: an 8 vCPU / 32 GB server and about 11 GB per day of raw flows (7 days of raw data; aggregates up to 25 months per subscriber and 5 years per node).

readonly.title: Never writes to the router
readonly.body: Its RouterOS user is read-only. You apply the recommended commands, if you want to.

isolation.title: Every ISP isolated
isolation.body: At every layer: row policies in PostgreSQL and ClickHouse, tenant-scoped events and ISP-scoped tokens.

access.title: Protected access
access.body: TOTP 2FA for administrators and rate limiting on the real client IP, also behind a proxy.

secrets.title: Encrypted credentials
secrets.body: Integration credentials are stored encrypted and are write-only.

pii.title: Less personal data
pii.body: Logs and the diagnostic bundle mask subscriber IPs.

local.title: On your server
local.body: Data stays in your installation. Off-site copies over SFTP are optional.

routers.a: MikroTik with RouterOS 7.12 or later. RouterOS 6 is not supported.

changes.q: Does Horus change anything on my router?
changes.a: No. You paste the onboarding script yourself: it creates the WireGuard tunnel, enables flow export and a read-only user. Horus never writes to the router, and the guide explains how to undo everything.

server.a: A clean Debian 12 or 13 (amd64). From 4 cores, 8 GB RAM and 100 GB SSD for about 300 subscribers, up to 8 cores, 32 GB and 500 GB NVMe for about 10,000.

domain.a: No. You can use just the server IP, a domain or subdomain with an automatic certificate, or put it behind your own proxy, such as Nginx Proxy Manager.

nat.q: Does it work with NAT on the router?
nat.a: Yes. With NAT on the main router, Horus uses IPFIX post-NAT fields to tell which subscriber each flow belongs to. It has been verified with a real MikroTik.

ipv6.a: Yes. IPv4 and IPv6 are treated as separate subscribers, and IPv6 is grouped by delegated prefix (/64 by default).

offline.q: Can it be installed without Internet access?
offline.a: Yes, with the offline installation package.

screenshots.q: Are the screenshots from real subscribers?
screenshots.a: No. Every screenshot on this page uses simulated data.
